subject: Biology
text: Define humoral immune response. Name two types of antibodies produced during humoral immune response.
modelAnswer: Humoral immune response is the production of antibodies by B-lymphocytes (plasma cells) in response to antigens circulating in blood and lymph. Two types of antibodies: (1) IgM – produced first during primary immune response; (2) IgG – produced in higher amounts during secondary immune response and provides long-term immunity.

subject: Biology
text: State the role of Lactobacillus in curd preparation. Mention two health benefits of consuming curd.
modelAnswer: Lactobacillus (LAB – Lactic Acid Bacteria) ferments lactose in milk producing lactic acid, which lowers pH, coagulates and partially digests milk proteins, converting milk to curd. Health benefits: (1) Increases nutritional value by producing Vitamin B12; (2) Checks the growth of harmful microbes in the gut, keeping the gut healthy.

subject: Biology
text: Identify the disease: a person develops itchy, inflamed circular patches on skin. Name two causative organisms and mode of transmission.
modelAnswer: Disease: Ringworm (Dermatophytosis). Causative organisms: (1) Microsporum, (2) Trichophyton (or Epidermophyton). Mode of transmission: Direct contact with infected person's skin/clothing/towels/soil; also indirect contact with contaminated objects.
keyPoints: Direct contact with infected person or contaminated objects

subject: Biology
text: A person working in a garden develops sneezing and watery eyes. Name the immune component responsible, the chemical released, and the medicine used to get relief.
modelAnswer: Immune component: Mast cells (which release chemicals on encountering allergen). Chemical released: Histamine (also serotonin and leukotrienes). Medicine: Antihistamines (anti-allergic drugs such as diphenhydramine). The allergens bind to IgE antibodies on mast cells triggering degranulation.

subject: Biology
text: A patient has fever, chills, sweating and a toxic substance in blood. Identify the disease and explain why fever recurs at regular intervals.
modelAnswer: Disease: Malaria (caused by Plasmodium). Recurring fever explanation: The malarial parasite undergoes schizogony inside RBCs, bursting them in a cyclic pattern – Plasmodium vivax causes fever every 48 h (tertian malaria); P. malariae every 72 h (quartan malaria). Each cycle of RBC rupture releases merozoites and toxins (haemozoin), causing a bout of fever and chills.
keyPoints: Cyclic RBC rupture releases merozoites and haemozoin causing recurring fever

subject: Biology
text: Name the microbial source and mode of action of: (i) Cyclosporin A, (ii) Streptokinase.
modelAnswer: (i) Cyclosporin A: Source – Trichoderma polysporum (fungus). Mode of action – immunosuppressive drug; suppresses the immune response, used to prevent organ-transplant rejection. (ii) Streptokinase: Source – Streptococcus bacterium. Mode of action – clot-buster (thrombolytic); dissolves blood clots in blood vessels of patients with myocardial infarction.
keyPoints: Cyclosporin A from Trichoderma polysporum – immunosuppressant

subject: Biology
text: Identify the disease: Patient has fever, weight loss, and repeated infections. How does the causative virus affect the immune system? Name two modes of transmission.
modelAnswer: Disease: AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) caused by HIV. Effect on immune system: HIV infects and destroys Helper T-lymphocytes (CD4+ T-cells), progressively reducing their count, leading to immunodeficiency. Without helper T-cells, the patient cannot mount immune responses. Modes of transmission: (1) Sexual contact with infected person; (2) Sharing infected needles/syringes; (3) Infected blood transfusion; (4) From infected mother to child (trans-placental or through breast milk).
keyPoints: Sexual contact, sharing needles, blood transfusion, mother to child

subject: Biology
text: How does the human body protect itself against inhaled dust particles and pathogens? Name two types of barriers involved.
modelAnswer: Protection: (1) Mucus secreted by the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract traps dust and microbes; (2) Cilia sweep the trapped material away from the lungs. Two barrier types: (i) Physical barriers – mucus, ciliated epithelium (also skin, earwax); (ii) Physiological barriers – acid in stomach (HCl), lysozyme in saliva and tears.

subject: Biology
text: Name the cells HIV first attacks. Explain how the virus replicates inside these cells to cause immunodeficiency.
modelAnswer: HIV first attacks Helper T-lymphocytes (CD4+ T-cells / TH cells). Replication: HIV enters the cell, uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA from its RNA genome, which integrates into the host cell DNA (provirus). This provirus uses host machinery to produce new virus particles that bud off and infect more T-cells. Progressive destruction of Helper T-cells leads to immunodeficiency.
keyPoints: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA

subject: Biology
text: Differentiate between active immunity and passive immunity. What is a vaccine?
modelAnswer: Active immunity: produced by the body itself when exposed to antigens (pathogens/vaccines); slow, long-lasting. Passive immunity: antibodies produced outside and transferred into the body (e.g., antitoxin injection, mother's milk); immediate but short-lived. Vaccine: a preparation of weakened/killed pathogens or their antigens that stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing disease.
keyPoints: Vaccine stimulates immune system with safe antigen

subject: Biology
text: State the source and role of histamine and interferons in providing defence against infection in the human body.
modelAnswer: Histamine: Source – mast cells (and basophils). Role – released during inflammatory/allergic response; causes vasodilation, increases capillary permeability, attracts phagocytes to the site of infection. Interferons: Source – virus-infected cells. Role – proteins secreted by virus-infected cells that protect non-infected neighbouring cells by inhibiting viral replication inside them; effective against viral infections.
keyPoints: Histamine from mast cells – vasodilation, increased permeability
Interferons from virus-infected cells – inhibit viral replication in neighbouring cells

subject: Biology
text: A person is prescribed a rabies antitoxin injection after a dog bite, while another person receives a rabies vaccine before potential exposure. (a) Identify the type of immunity conferred in each case. (b) Differentiate between active and passive immunity.
modelAnswer: (a) Antitoxin injection → Passive immunity (ready-made antibodies given). Rabies vaccine → Active immunity (stimulates body to produce its own antibodies). (b) Active immunity: produced by the individual's own immune system in response to antigen; slow to develop but long-lasting and has memory. Passive immunity: antibodies produced externally and transferred; provides immediate protection but is short-lived and has no memory.

subject: Biology
text: Draw the life cycle of malarial parasite (Plasmodium) inside the human body in the form of a flowchart.
modelAnswer: Sporozoites injected by Anopheles mosquito → Enter liver cells (hepatocytes) → Multiply (exo-erythrocytic schizogony) → Merozoites released → Enter RBCs → Multiply (erythrocytic schizogony) → Erythrocytic merozoites → Rupture RBCs → Some form gametocytes → taken up by mosquito during next blood meal. The cyclic rupture of RBCs causes recurring fever.

subject: Biology
text: Do all pollen grains remain viable for the same length of time? Give one example each of a plant with short and long pollen viability. How are pollen grains preserved in pollen banks?
modelAnswer: No, pollen viability varies greatly. Short viability: rice and wheat pollen remain viable for only 30 minutes. Long viability: pollen of some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae remain viable for months. Preservation in pollen banks: pollen grains can be stored for years in liquid nitrogen (–196°C) with suitable preservatives – used in crop breeding programmes.

subject: Biology
text: Differentiate between wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers. Give one example of each.
modelAnswer: Wind-pollinated (anemophilous): flowers small, non-showy, no scent/nectar, pollen light, smooth and produced in large quantities, stigma large/feathery. Example: maize/corn (Zea mays). Insect-pollinated (entomophilous): flowers large, brightly coloured, fragrant, produce nectar, pollen sticky/spiny, stigma small and sticky. Example: rose.
keyPoints: Wind: small, no petals/scent, light pollen in large quantities, feathery stigma
Insect: colourful, fragrant, nectar, sticky pollen, sticky stigma

subject: Biology
text: What are apomictic seeds? Describe two different ways in which apomictic seeds develop. What is the advantage of apomictic seeds for farmers?
modelAnswer: Apomictic seeds are seeds produced without fertilization (no fusion of gametes). Two ways of development: (1) Diploid egg cell develops into embryo without fertilization (diplospory/agamospermy); (2) Nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac develop into embryos (nucellar polyembryony – e.g., mango, Citrus). Advantage: Seeds are genetically identical to the mother plant, preserving hybrid vigour generation after generation – farmers do not need to buy new hybrid seeds each year.
keyPoints: Diploid egg → embryo; nucellar cells → embryo
Genetically identical to mother – hybrid vigour maintained

subject: Biology
text: List any three outbreeding devices that flowering plants have developed for cross-pollination and explain how they promote cross-pollination.
modelAnswer: (1) Dichogamy: pollen release and stigma receptivity occur at different times in the same flower – prevents self-pollination within the flower. (2) Self-incompatibility (herkogamy): pollen of the same plant is unable to germinate on the stigma due to genetic/biochemical barriers. (3) Dioecy: male and female flowers are on separate plants (e.g., papaya, date palm) – self-pollination is impossible. (Also: protandry/protogyny, heterostyly.)
keyPoints: Dichogamy – different timing of pollen release and stigma receptivity

subject: Biology
text: State the functions of each of the following: (i) Tassels of a corn cob, (ii) Scutellum.
modelAnswer: (i) Tassels of corn cob: Tassels are the male inflorescence at the top of the corn plant. They produce and release large amounts of pollen grains for wind pollination. (ii) Scutellum: The scutellum (also called cotyledon of monocot seeds) is a shield-shaped structure in the embryo of grass/cereal seeds (monocots). It secretes enzymes (such as amylase) that digest the stored food in the endosperm and absorbs the nutrients for the growing seedling during germination.
keyPoints: Tassels = male inflorescence releasing pollen for wind pollination
Scutellum = cotyledon of monocot; absorbs digested nutrients from endosperm during germination

subject: Biology
text: At which stage of follicle development does the primary oocyte undergo its first meiotic division? Name the products formed.
modelAnswer: The primary oocyte completes meiosis I (first meiotic division) inside the Graafian follicle just before ovulation. Products: (1) A large secondary oocyte (receives most of the cytoplasm), and (2) A small first polar body (receives very little cytoplasm) – both are haploid cells.
keyPoints: Meiosis I completed inside Graafian follicle before ovulation
Products: secondary oocyte + first polar body

subject: Biology
text: Name the muscular and glandular layers of the female uterus. State one function of each.
modelAnswer: Muscular layer: Myometrium. Function – contracts strongly during parturition (childbirth) to expel the baby. Glandular layer: Endometrium. Function – provides nutrition to the implanted embryo; undergoes cyclic changes during the menstrual cycle; participates in placenta formation.
keyPoints: Endometrium = glandular; nourishes embryo, undergoes cyclic changes

subject: Biology
text: State the connection between the placenta and the foetus. How does the placenta provide nutritional and hormonal support?
modelAnswer: Connection: Placenta connects the foetus to the uterine wall via the umbilical cord. Nutritional support: Oxygen and nutrients pass from maternal blood to foetal blood across the placental barrier; waste products (CO2, urea) pass from foetus to mother. Hormonal support: Placenta secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), progesterone, estrogens, and human placental lactogen (hPL) to maintain pregnancy.
keyPoints: Nutrients and O2 pass to foetus; CO2 and urea removed

subject: Biology
text: Draw a schematic representation of oogenesis in human females, indicating the chromosome number at each stage.
modelAnswer: Oogonium (2n=46) → [mitosis] → Primary oocyte (2n=46) → [Meiosis I] → Secondary oocyte (n=23) + 1st polar body (n=23) → [Meiosis II, completed only after fertilization] → Ovum (n=23) + 2nd polar body (n=23). Note: secondary oocyte is ovulated and meiosis II is completed only if fertilization occurs.
keyPoints: Meiosis I → secondary oocyte n + 1st polar body
Meiosis II (after fertilization) → ovum n + 2nd polar body

subject: Biology
text: Name the lymphoid organ that acts as a large reservoir of erythrocytes. Explain its role as a lymphoid organ.
modelAnswer: Spleen is the largest lymphoid organ and acts as a reservoir of erythrocytes. Role as lymphoid organ: (1) Contains lymphocytes and macrophages that trap and destroy blood-borne microbes and antigens; (2) Filters blood, removing old/damaged RBCs; (3) Produces antibodies in immune responses.
keyPoints: Contains lymphocytes and macrophages for immune response

subject: Biology
text: State the role of thymus as a lymphoid organ. Name the cells released from it and mention their functions.
modelAnswer: Thymus: A bilobed organ in the thorax behind the sternum. Role: It is the primary lymphoid organ where T-lymphocytes mature and become immunocompetent. It secretes thymosins which promote differentiation of T-cells. Cells released: T-lymphocytes (T-cells). Functions: T-cells mediate cell-mediated immunity – cytotoxic T-cells kill virus-infected/cancerous cells; helper T-cells activate other immune cells.
keyPoints: Cytotoxic T-cells kill infected cells; helper T-cells activate immune response

subject: Biology
text: (a) Draw a labelled diagram of a human ovum prior to fertilization labelling any four parts. (b) How is polyspermy avoided after fertilization?
modelAnswer: (a) Diagram labels: Corona radiata (outermost layer of follicle cells), Zona pellucida (glycoprotein layer), Plasma membrane/oolemma, Cytoplasm/ooplasm (with yolk), Nucleus (with first polar body in perivitelline space). (b) Polyspermy prevention: Upon entry of one sperm, cortical granules beneath the egg plasma membrane fuse with the membrane and release enzymes into the perivitelline space → zona reaction: zona pellucida hardens (becomes zona reaction block) → prevents additional sperms from penetrating.
keyPoints: Corona radiata, zona pellucida, plasma membrane, nucleus
Cortical granules released on sperm entry
Zona reaction hardens ZP blocking further sperm

subject: Biology
text: Name the embryonic stage that gets implanted in the human uterus. Draw a labelled diagram and state the functions of any two labelled parts.
modelAnswer: Blastocyst gets implanted in the uterine endometrium. Diagram: Trophoblast (outer layer) + Inner cell mass (embryoblast). Functions: (1) Trophoblast – attaches to endometrium; later forms placenta and foetal membranes; secretes hCG. (2) Inner cell mass (embryoblast) – gives rise to the embryo proper; differentiates into all tissues and organs of the foetus.
keyPoints: Inner cell mass – forms embryo proper

subject: Biology
text: Draw a sectional view of a seminiferous tubule of a human and label the following cells: (i) Cells that divide by mitosis to increase their number, (ii) Cells that undergo meiosis I, (iii) Cells that undergo meiosis II, (iv) Cells that help in spermiogenesis. Also mention the role of Leydig cells.
modelAnswer: (i) Spermatogonia – divide mitotically to maintain stem cell pool. (ii) Primary spermatocytes – undergo meiosis I. (iii) Secondary spermatocytes – undergo meiosis II. (iv) Sertoli cells (nurse cells) – support and nourish developing spermatids during spermiogenesis; phagocytose excess cytoplasm. Role of Leydig cells (interstitial cells): located in interstitial tissue between seminiferous tubules; secrete male sex hormone testosterone.

subject: Biology
text: Mention the sites of secretion and functions of GnRH and FSH during spermatogenesis.
modelAnswer: GnRH (Gonadotropin Releasing Hormone): Site – hypothalamus. Function – stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete gonadotropins LH and FSH. FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone): Site – anterior pituitary. Function – acts on Sertoli cells in seminiferous tubules, stimulating them to secrete factors essential for spermiogenesis (maturation of spermatids to spermatozoa); also stimulates spermatogenesis.
keyPoints: GnRH from hypothalamus – triggers pituitary to release LH and FSH
FSH from anterior pituitary – acts on Sertoli cells, stimulates spermiogenesis

subject: Biology
text: What are the menstrual and follicular phases of the menstrual cycle? What events occur at ovulation from the Graafian follicle?
modelAnswer: Menstrual phase (Day 1–5): Shedding of the endometrium (menstruation) due to fall in progesterone and estrogen if fertilization does not occur. Follicular (proliferative) phase (Day 6–13): FSH stimulates growth of Graafian follicle; estrogen secretion causes endometrial proliferation. Ovulation: On Day 14, LH surge causes rupture of Graafian follicle releasing secondary oocyte. The ruptured follicle becomes corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to maintain endometrium.
keyPoints: Menstrual phase: endometrium shed, hormone levels fall
Follicular phase: Graafian follicle grows, estrogen rises
Ovulation Day 14: LH surge, secondary oocyte released; corpus luteum formed

subject: Biology
text: Why are STIs (Sexually Transmitted Infections) often not detected in time? Name two complications that can arise in later stages if untreated.
modelAnswer: STIs are often not detected in time because: (1) Most STIs are asymptomatic in early stages – no noticeable signs; (2) Social stigma prevents people from seeking medical help promptly. Two complications in later stages: (1) Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), which can lead to infertility; (2) Increased risk of certain cancers (e.g., cervical cancer from HPV, liver cancer from Hepatitis B); (3) HIV can lead to AIDS.

subject: Biology
text: Define amniocentesis. Why has the government imposed a statutory ban on it despite its medical importance?
modelAnswer: Amniocentesis: A technique used for foetal sex determination and detection of chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., Down syndrome) by analysing amniotic fluid withdrawn from the amniotic sac using a syringe. Medical importance: Detects genetic disorders, metabolic disorders and open neural tube defects in the foetus. Reason for ban: The technique was being widely misused for female foetal sex determination followed by female foeticide (selective abortion of female foetuses), contributing to falling female sex ratio.
keyPoints: Foetal fluid analysis for genetic abnormalities
Banned because misused for sex-selective female foeticide

subject: Biology
text: How do 'implants' act as an effective method of contraception in human females? Mention one advantage of implants over contraceptive pills.
modelAnswer: Implants are small progestogen-releasing capsules/rods inserted subcutaneously (under skin), usually in the upper arm. They prevent pregnancy by: suppressing ovulation, thickening cervical mucus (preventing sperm entry), and thinning endometrium (preventing implantation). Advantage over pills: Implants are long-acting (effective for 3–5 years) and once inserted require no daily attention, unlike oral contraceptive pills which must be taken daily and risk non-compliance.
keyPoints: Suppresses ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, thins endometrium
Advantage: long-acting (3–5 years), no daily compliance needed

subject: Biology
text: Name two copper-releasing IUDs. Why are copper-releasing IUDs effective contraceptives?
modelAnswer: Two copper-releasing IUDs: CuT (Copper-T) and Cu7 (Copper-7) / Multiload 375. Mechanism of effectiveness: (1) Copper ions released are spermicidal (toxic to sperm), reducing their motility and fertilizing capacity; (2) The IUD creates a hostile environment in the uterus; (3) Some IUDs also make the uterus unsuitable for implantation. Together these effects make them highly effective long-term contraceptives.

subject: Biology
text: What is Saheli? How does it differ from other oral contraceptive pills in terms of composition and advantage?
modelAnswer: Saheli is a non-steroidal oral contraceptive pill developed by CDRI Lucknow, India. Composition: Contains centchroman (ormeloxifene), a non-steroidal anti-estrogen – unlike conventional oral pills which contain synthetic estrogen and/or progestogen (steroids). Advantage: (1) Taken once a week (not daily); (2) Being non-steroidal, it has fewer side effects; (3) High contraceptive efficacy; (4) First non-steroidal oral contraceptive.
keyPoints: Once a week, fewer side effects than steroid-based pills

subject: Biology
text: What is pedigree analysis? State its importance. What does the following pedigree pattern indicate about the type of inheritance?
modelAnswer: Pedigree analysis is the study of the inheritance pattern of a trait in a family across several generations using a standardised chart. Importance: (1) Helps determine whether a trait is dominant or recessive, autosomal or sex-linked; (2) Helps predict the probability of a trait appearing in offspring; (3) Used in genetic counselling for hereditary diseases. A pedigree in which affected males are more frequent and trait passes through carrier females suggests X-linked recessive inheritance (e.g., haemophilia, colour blindness).
keyPoints: Pedigree tracks trait inheritance across generations

subject: Biology
text: Analyse the sex determination mechanisms in (i) humans (XO/XX) and (ii) birds (ZW/ZZ). State which sex is heterogametic in each case.
modelAnswer: (i) Humans: Males are XY, females are XX. Males produce two types of gametes (X-bearing and Y-bearing sperm) → males are heterogametic. XX females are homogametic. The sex of the offspring is determined by which sperm fertilizes the egg. (ii) Birds: Males are ZZ, females are ZW. Females produce two types of gametes (Z-bearing and W-bearing eggs) → females are heterogametic. ZZ males are homogametic.
keyPoints: Human males XY – heterogametic; females XX – homogametic
Bird females ZW – heterogametic; males ZZ – homogametic

subject: Biology
text: Why did Mendel's work published in 1865 remain unrecognised for about 35 years? Give four reasons.
modelAnswer: (1) His paper was published in a local journal (Proceedings of Natural History Society) with limited circulation. (2) Most scientists of his time could not appreciate statistical analysis applied to biology. (3) He proposed the concept of discrete hereditary factors (genes) which was not accepted – prevailing theory was blending inheritance. (4) His work was ahead of its time; cell biology and meiosis were not yet understood, so the physical basis of his factors was unknown.
keyPoints: Statistical analysis in biology not appreciated
Concept of discrete factors not accepted (blending inheritance prevalent)

subject: Biology
text: Give four reasons why Mendel succeeded in his experiments with garden pea (Pisum sativum).
modelAnswer: (1) Choice of garden pea: easily cultivable, normally self-fertilising, short life span with distinct generations. (2) Selected 7 pairs of contrasting characters with clear-cut alternatives (no blending). (3) Maintained detailed statistical records of large numbers of offspring over many generations. (4) Selected traits located on different chromosomes (independently assorting) – allowing him to observe ratios clearly. He was also a skilled and systematic observer.
keyPoints: Large sample size and statistical analysis
Traits on different chromosomes for clear ratios

subject: Biology
text: A haemophilic man marries a normal woman whose father was haemophilic. (i) Work out the cross for this couple. (ii) What is the probability that their sons will be haemophilic? (iii) Can their daughter be haemophilic?
modelAnswer: Haemophilic man: X^h Y. Normal woman with haemophilic father: X^H X^h (carrier). Cross: X^h Y × X^H X^h → offspring: X^H X^h (carrier daughter), X^h X^h (haemophilic daughter), X^H Y (normal son), X^h Y (haemophilic son). (i) 1:1:1:1 ratio. (ii) 50% (1 in 2) of sons will be haemophilic. (iii) Yes, daughters can be haemophilic – 50% chance (X^h X^h), making this one of the rare cases where a female is haemophilic.
keyPoints: Haemophilic man: X^hY; carrier woman: X^H X^h

subject: Biology
text: What are multiple alleles? How do they differ from dominant-recessive allele pairs? Explain with reference to ABO blood groups: list all genotypes and corresponding phenotypes.
modelAnswer: Multiple alleles: When a gene has more than two allelic forms in a population (though any individual has only two). They differ from dominant-recessive pairs in that multiple alleles show co-dominance (both expressed simultaneously). ABO blood group gene (I): has three alleles – I^A, I^B, i. Genotypes and phenotypes: I^A I^A or I^A i → Blood group A; I^B I^B or I^B i → Blood group B; I^A I^B → Blood group AB (co-dominant); ii → Blood group O.
keyPoints: Multiple alleles: >2 forms of same gene in population
ABO: I^A I^A/I^A i = A; I^B I^B/I^B i = B; I^A I^B = AB; ii = O

subject: Biology
text: What is the haemoglobin mutation in sickle cell anaemia? What is the condition called and what are its effects on the patient?
modelAnswer: Mutation: In the beta-globin gene of haemoglobin, a single nucleotide change (GAG → GTG) causes substitution of glutamic acid by valine at position 6. Condition: Sickle Cell Anaemia (autosomal recessive). Effects: RBCs become sickle-shaped under low oxygen, leading to (1) haemolytic anaemia (RBCs rupture), causing fatigue and weakness; (2) blockage of capillaries causing pain crisis (vaso-occlusive crisis), tissue damage, and organ failure.
keyPoints: GAG→GTG mutation; glutamic acid→valine in beta-globin
Sickle-shaped RBCs → haemolysis and capillary blockage

subject: Biology
text: Explain polygenic inheritance with a suitable example.
modelAnswer: Polygenic inheritance: A trait controlled by two or more genes (polygenes), each contributing additively to the phenotype. The phenotype shows continuous variation. Example: Skin colour in humans – controlled by at least 3 genes (A, B, C), each with two alleles. More dominant alleles → more melanin → darker skin. Possible phenotypes range from very dark (AABBCC) to very light (aabbcc) with many intermediate shades. When plotted, offspring show a bell-shaped normal distribution curve of phenotypes.
keyPoints: Skin colour: 3 gene pairs; more dominant alleles = more melanin

subject: Biology
text: The sequence 5'-GAATTC-3' is called a palindromic sequence. What are such sequences called in restriction enzyme nomenclature? Name the enzyme that recognises this site and explain how it functions.
modelAnswer: Such sequences are called palindromic recognition sequences. The enzyme: EcoRI. How it functions: EcoRI recognises the palindromic sequence GAATTC on both strands and cuts between G and AATTC on each strand, creating staggered cuts. This produces fragments with single-stranded overhangs called 'sticky ends' (cohesive ends: 5'-AATT-3'), which can hydrogen-bond with complementary sticky ends of other DNA fragments cut by the same enzyme, facilitating recombinant DNA formation.

subject: Biology
text: Derive the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium expression p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Name two factors that can disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
modelAnswer: If allele A has frequency p and allele a has frequency q (p + q = 1), random mating produces: AA (p × p = p²), Aa (p × q + q × p = 2pq), aa (q × q = q²). Sum = p² + 2pq + q² = (p + q)² = 1. Two factors disturbing equilibrium: (1) Natural selection – differential survival of genotypes; (2) Genetic drift – random changes in allele frequency in small populations; others include mutation, gene flow/migration, non-random mating.
keyPoints: Disturbed by: natural selection, genetic drift, mutation, gene flow

subject: Biology
text: In a population, 36% individuals have blue eyes (recessive, bb). Using Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, calculate: (i) frequency of allele B, (ii) % heterozygous individuals, (iii) % homozygous dominant individuals.
modelAnswer: q² = 0.36 (blue eyes, bb) → q = 0.6; p = 1 – 0.6 = 0.4. (i) Frequency of allele B (p) = 0.4. (ii) Heterozygous (Bb) = 2pq = 2 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.48 = 48%. (iii) Homozygous dominant (BB) = p² = 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16 = 16%.

subject: Biology
text: Explain the process of gel electrophoresis for separation of DNA fragments. Why are DNA fragments not visible after electrophoresis? How can they be visualised and how can a specific band be collected?
modelAnswer: Gel electrophoresis: DNA fragments are loaded onto agarose gel; electric current applied – negatively charged DNA migrates toward anode; smaller fragments travel faster and farther. Fragments not visible: DNA is colourless and not fluorescent. Visualisation: Gel is stained with ethidium bromide (EtBr), which intercalates into DNA; under UV light, bright orange/pink bands appear. Collection: The band corresponding to desired fragment is cut out from gel (eluted); DNA is extracted and purified for downstream applications.
keyPoints: Agarose gel, electric field; smaller fragments move farther
Stained with ethidium bromide; visualised under UV
Desired band cut out and DNA eluted

subject: Biology
text: Draw a labelled diagram of a replicating fork showing polarity. Why does DNA replication occur at such a fork?
modelAnswer: Replicating fork (Y-shaped): Leading strand (template 3'→5') synthesized continuously in 5'→3' direction toward the fork; lagging strand (template 5'→3') synthesized discontinuously in short Okazaki fragments away from the fork. Why fork structure: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in 5'→3' direction; when the double helix unwinds at the fork, both templates are exposed simultaneously, allowing simultaneous synthesis of both strands. The fork represents the point of unwinding by helicase.
keyPoints: DNA pol adds only in 5'→3' direction

subject: Biology
text: What is the significance of repetitive sequences in the human genome? What do they tell us about chromosome structure?
modelAnswer: Significance: Repetitive DNA sequences (making up a large portion of human genome) do not directly code for proteins. They illuminate chromosome structure: (1) Satellite DNA (tandem repeats at centromeres and telomeres) plays structural roles in chromosome organisation, segregation and protection of chromosome ends; (2) Repetitive sequences are used in DNA fingerprinting because their number varies between individuals (VNTRs); (3) They play roles in genome regulation and evolution.
keyPoints: Satellite DNA at centromeres/telomeres – structural roles

subject: Biology
text: One of the salient features of the genetic code is that it is nearly universal. Mention two exceptions to this rule. Why are some codons said to be degenerate?
modelAnswer: Two exceptions to universality: (1) UGA in mitochondria codes for tryptophan (not a stop codon); (2) AUA in mitochondria codes for methionine (not isoleucine as in cytoplasmic ribosomes). Other examples: Mycoplasma – UGA codes for tryptophan. Degenerate codons: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon (synonymous codons) – e.g., leucine is coded by 6 codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG). These codons are called degenerate because multiple codons specify the same amino acid.
keyPoints: Degenerate = one amino acid has multiple codons (synonymous codons)

subject: Biology
text: What was Henking's observation that led to the discovery of sex chromosomes? Explain the significance of this observation.
modelAnswer: Henking (1891) observed that during spermatogenesis in some insects, a specific nuclear element (chromatin body) was transferred to only 50% of the sperms after cell division. He labelled this element 'X body' (X for unknown). Later scientists found that 50% of sperm carried this element (X) and 50% did not → two types of sperm. This was significant because it explained why offspring are produced in a 1:1 sex ratio – eggs fertilized by X-carrying sperm develop as females (XX) and those fertilized by X-less sperm develop as males (XO or XY).
keyPoints: Henking observed X body transferred to only 50% of sperm
Two types of sperm (X-bearing and not)
Led to discovery of sex chromosomes

subject: Biology
text: Explain industrial melanism as an evidence for natural selection. What change occurred in the population of Biston betularia after industrialisation?
modelAnswer: Before industrialisation, light-coloured (peppered) moths were camouflaged on lichen-covered trees and dark (melanised) moths were rare (visible to predators). After industrialisation: soot covered tree bark → light moths became conspicuous and dark moths were camouflaged. Predators ate more light moths; dark moths survived and reproduced more. Result: frequency of dark (melanised) moths increased dramatically in industrial areas while light moths decreased. This demonstrated natural selection (directional selection) in action.
keyPoints: Dark moths better camouflaged → higher survival
Natural selection led to increased frequency of dark moths

subject: Biology
text: What is adaptive radiation? Explain with one example from Darwin's observations.
modelAnswer: Adaptive radiation: The process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area from a single ancestral species, diverging to exploit different ecological niches (habitats). Example: Darwin's finches in the Galapagos Islands – a single ancestral finch species colonised the islands; different populations evolved different beak shapes (small seed-eaters, large seed-crackers, insect-eaters, cactus-feeders) adapted to available food sources, giving rise to 14+ distinct species.
keyPoints: Single ancestor → multiple species exploiting different niches
Darwin's finches: 14 species from one ancestor
Different beak shapes adapted to different food sources

subject: Biology
text: Describe the three ways in which natural selection can operate on a population. Draw graphs to illustrate each.
modelAnswer: (1) Stabilising selection: Favours the average phenotype; reduces variation; individuals at both extremes are selected against. Graph: normal curve becomes narrower. Example: birth weight in humans. (2) Directional selection: Favours one extreme phenotype; shifts the population mean in one direction. Graph: bell curve shifts toward one extreme. Example: industrial melanism in moths. (3) Disruptive selection: Favours both extreme phenotypes and selects against the average; splits the population. Graph: bimodal distribution. Example: beak size in African seedcrackers.
keyPoints: Directional: favours one extreme, shifts mean
Disruptive: favours both extremes, bimodal distribution

subject: Biology
text: Identify the hominid with a brain capacity of 900 cc, and the one with 650–800 cc brain capacity. Rearrange these in correct evolutionary order: Australopithecus, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Homo neanderthalensis.
modelAnswer: 900 cc brain capacity: Homo erectus. 650–800 cc brain capacity: Homo habilis. Correct evolutionary order: Australopithecus (4 mya) → Homo habilis (2 mya) → Homo erectus (1.5 mya) → Homo neanderthalensis (0.1 mya) → Homo sapiens.
keyPoints: Evolutionary order: Australopithecus → H. habilis → H. erectus → H. neanderthalensis

chapter: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
subject: Biology
text: How does a farmer use seed dormancy to advantage? Differentiate between the type of dormancy in pea seeds versus castor seeds.
modelAnswer: Farmer's use: Seed dormancy allows farmers to harvest seeds and store them safely without germination; seeds can be stored for planting in the next season. Pea seeds (exogenous dormancy): Dormancy is due to the hard, impermeable seed coat that prevents water/oxygen entry – overcome by scarification or soaking. Castor seeds (endogenous dormancy): Dormancy is due to the presence of inhibitors (abscisic acid) in the embryo – overcome by after-ripening or cold stratification.
keyPoints: Dormancy allows safe storage of seeds

chapter: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
subject: Biology
text: State two advantages of micropropagation (tissue culture). Give two examples of plants produced commercially through this technique.
modelAnswer: Two advantages: (1) Millions of plants can be produced in a short time from small amount of plant material; (2) Produces disease-free (pathogen-free) plants; identical (clonal) copies of desirable varieties. Examples of commercial micropropagation: (1) Tomato – disease-free plants; (2) Banana – disease-free, uniform plants for commercial farming; (3) Orchids; (4) Potato (virus-free plants).
keyPoints: Rapid propagation of millions of plants

chapter: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
subject: Biology
text: How can a healthy, virus-free plant be obtained from a virus-infected sugarcane plant? Explain the technique involved.
modelAnswer: Meristem culture (Shoot tip culture/Apical meristem culture): The meristematic cells at the shoot apex are not infected by virus even in a diseased plant, because viruses spread through vascular tissue which has not yet differentiated in the meristem. Process: (1) Excise shoot apical meristem (0.1–0.5 mm) under sterile conditions; (2) Culture on nutrient medium; (3) The meristem differentiates and grows into a complete plantlet; (4) The plantlet is tested for virus, found virus-free, and multiplied.
keyPoints: Apical meristem is virus-free (vascular tissue absent)
Excised meristem cultured on nutrient medium

chapter: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
subject: Biology
text: What is the Bt-toxin gene in Bt corn? Explain the effect of Bt spores on a pest. How did GM field 'B' develop resistance to Bt toxin?
modelAnswer: Bt-toxin gene: cry gene (crystalline protein gene) from Bacillus thuringiensis. Effect on pest: Bt spores/crystals are ingested by the insect larva; in the alkaline gut environment, the protoxin is converted to active toxin; the toxin binds to specific receptors in midgut epithelial cells, creating pores that lyse cells, causing the insect to stop feeding and die. Resistance development (GM field B): Farmers in one field planted only Bt corn → insects were exposed to continuous high selection pressure → genetic variants with altered/absent receptors were selected → resistant insects survived and reproduced → resistant population built up. Refuge strategy (non-Bt plants) would have prevented this.
keyPoints: Alkaline gut activates protoxin → pores in midgut cells → insect death
Resistance from continuous Bt exposure, selecting receptor mutants; no refuge strategy

subject: Biology
text: Describe the processes occurring in sewage treatment after significant BOD reduction has been achieved in secondary treatment. What is the important outcome?
modelAnswer: After secondary treatment (biological treatment) significantly reduces BOD: (1) Effluent undergoes sedimentation – biomass settles as secondary sludge; (2) Supernatant (secondary effluent) with low BOD is released after tertiary treatment (optional: chlorination/UV to kill pathogens). Primary and secondary sludge are treated by anaerobic sludge digestion – anaerobic bacteria digest the organic matter, producing biogas (CH4 + CO2) which can be used as fuel. Important outcome: Effluent BOD is reduced to safe levels for release into water bodies; biogas is a valuable energy by-product.
keyPoints: Effluent with low BOD safely released

subject: Biology
text: Three water samples have BOD values of 30 mg/L, 8 mg/L, and 400 mg/L. Identify the most polluted sample. Assign likely sources to each BOD value.
modelAnswer: Most polluted: 400 mg/L (highest BOD = most organic matter = most microbial activity = most pollution). Assignment: 400 mg/L → raw sewage/untreated sewage water. 30 mg/L → river water receiving some organic input or secondary effluent. 8 mg/L → clean river water (very low pollution; BOD < 10 mg/L is considered clean). BOD (Biological Oxygen Demand) measures the oxygen required by microbes to decompose organic matter; higher BOD = more organic matter = more pollution.
keyPoints: 30 mg/L = secondary effluent / moderately polluted river

subject: Biology
text: Describe a biogas plant using cow dung. Does it need an inoculum? What happens to biowaste in the digester? Name the useful by-products.
modelAnswer: Biogas plant: A sealed tank/digester is filled with slurry (cow dung + water in ~1:1 ratio). No separate inoculum needed – cow dung naturally contains methanogenic bacteria (Methanobacterium) which initiate fermentation. In the digester: Anaerobic bacteria degrade organic matter (cellulose, proteins) in stages: hydrolysis → acidogenesis → acetogenesis → methanogenesis. Useful by-products: (1) Biogas – mixture of methane (~55–60%) + CO2 + traces of H2S, used as fuel for cooking and electricity; (2) Spent slurry – nutrient-rich sludge used as organic manure/fertiliser.
keyPoints: Cow dung slurry in anaerobic digester
No external inoculum – methanogenic bacteria naturally present in dung

subject: Biology
text: Who discovered penicillin? How was it discovered? Why is this discovery considered a milestone in medicine?
modelAnswer: Discovered by: Alexander Fleming (1928). How discovered: Fleming observed that a mould (Penicillium notatum) had accidentally contaminated a bacterial culture of Staphylococcus; around the mould colony, bacteria were not growing (clear zone). He concluded the mould was producing a substance that inhibited bacterial growth – he named it penicillin. Why it is a milestone: Penicillin was the first antibiotic discovered; it was effective against many pathogenic bacteria; its development and mass production (Chain and Florey) during WWII saved millions of lives from bacterial infections; it opened the era of antibiotic medicine.
keyPoints: Mould Penicillium notatum contaminated bacterial culture
Mould inhibited bacterial growth → antibiotic penicillin
First antibiotic; saved millions of lives

subject: Biology
text: Mention a product of human welfare obtained with the help of each of the following: (a) Saccharomyces cerevisiae, (b) Propionibacterium shermanii, (c) Aspergillus niger, (d) Trichoderma polysporum, (e) Acetobacter aceti, (f) Streptococcus.
modelAnswer: (a) Saccharomyces cerevisiae – ethanol (beer, wine); also baker's yeast for bread. (b) Propionibacterium shermanii – Swiss cheese (produces CO2 bubbles and propionic acid for flavour). (c) Aspergillus niger – citric acid (food preservative/flavouring) / gluconic acid. (d) Trichoderma polysporum – cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant drug). (e) Acetobacter aceti – acetic acid/vinegar. (f) Streptococcus – streptokinase (thrombolytic/clot-buster enzyme).

subject: Biology
text: Explain how Bacillus thuringiensis and Nucleopolyhedrovirus act as biocontrol agents.
modelAnswer: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt): This bacterium produces Bt toxin (δ-endotoxin/cry protein) as crystalline inclusions during sporulation. When insect larvae (lepidopterans, coleopterans) ingest Bt spores/crystals, the alkaline gut activates the toxin; it binds midgut receptors, creates pores → cell lysis → larva dies. Used as biopesticide spray or via transgenic crops (Bt crops). Nucleopolyhedrovirus (NPV): A baculovirus used as biocontrol agent for forest/crop pests. It infects and kills specific insects (lepidopteran pests); narrow host range, safe for non-target organisms, mammals and birds. Used in integrated pest management.
keyPoints: Bt: cry toxin activated in alkaline gut → pores in midgut → insect death
NPV: baculovirus infects and kills specific lepidopteran pests
Both are species-specific, safe for non-target organisms

subject: Biology
text: Explain microinjection and gene gun as methods of introducing alien DNA into host cells.
modelAnswer: Microinjection: Recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell using a fine glass micropipette (microinjector) under a microscope. Effective for introducing DNA into oocytes and embryonic cells of animals (used to produce transgenic animals). Gene gun (Biolistics): Tiny gold or tungsten particles coated with recombinant DNA are accelerated using high-pressure helium gas and shot into plant cells. The particles penetrate cell wall and membrane, delivering DNA. Used for plant transformation (also for animal cells and in DNA vaccines).
keyPoints: Microinjection: recombinant DNA injected into nucleus via glass micropipette
Gene gun: DNA-coated metal particles shot at high velocity into cells

subject: Biology
text: State the importance of 'ori' (origin of replication) in a cloning vector. Why is DNA Polymerase important in PCR?
modelAnswer: Ori (Origin of Replication): The specific sequence where DNA replication begins inside the host cell. The ori controls the copy number of the vector – vectors with high-copy ori produce many copies of foreign DNA. Without ori, the vector cannot replicate autonomously in the host cell and the foreign gene will not be amplified. DNA Polymerase in PCR: A thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus) is essential because PCR involves repeated cycles of heating to 94°C (denaturation). Taq pol survives these temperatures and extends primers to amplify the target DNA sequence.
keyPoints: Ori initiates replication; controls copy number
Without ori, vector cannot self-replicate in host
Taq polymerase is thermostable, survives 94°C PCR cycles
Extends primers to amplify target DNA

subject: Biology
text: In order to force bacteria to take up recombinant DNA, they must be made 'competent'. Explain how this is achieved.
modelAnswer: Bacteria are normally not permeable to DNA. To make them competent (able to take up DNA): (1) Treat bacterial cells with divalent cations (CaCl2 solution) which increases the permeability of the cell membrane by interacting with phospholipids; (2) Incubate cells with recombinant DNA on ice; (3) Brief heat shock at 42°C causes the DNA to enter the cell through transient membrane pores. Alternatively, electroporation (brief electric pulse) is used to create pores for DNA entry.
keyPoints: DNA + cells on ice, then 42°C heat shock
Allows bacterial cells to take up foreign/recombinant DNA

subject: Biology
text: Explain the importance of insertional inactivation in detecting recombinant DNA. Name the vector used for gene transfer to plant cells.
modelAnswer: Insertional inactivation: In plasmid pBR322, antibiotic resistance genes (ampicillin = bla and tetracycline = tet) are selectable markers. If foreign DNA is inserted into the tet gene (at restriction sites within tet), the tet gene is disrupted (insertionally inactivated). Recombinant selection: (1) Plate bacteria on ampicillin medium → all transformed bacteria survive (have plasmid); (2) Replica plate on tetracycline medium → recombinants fail to grow (tet gene disrupted) while non-recombinants grow. Vector for plant gene transfer: Ti plasmid (Tumour-inducing plasmid) of Agrobacterium tumefaciens – a natural plant pathogen that integrates T-DNA into the plant genome.
keyPoints: Foreign DNA inserted into tet gene disrupts tetracycline resistance
Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens for plant gene transfer

subject: Biology
text: State the role of 'ori' and 'restriction site' in the cloning vector pBR322.
modelAnswer: ori (Origin of Replication) in pBR322: The sequence where self-replication of the plasmid is initiated inside E. coli. It controls the copy number. Without ori, the vector cannot replicate independently in the host cell, so inserted foreign DNA would not be amplified. Restriction site in pBR322: Specific recognition sequences within antibiotic resistance genes (tet, bla) where restriction enzymes cut. Foreign DNA is inserted here using the same restriction enzyme → insertional inactivation of the antibiotic gene → enables identification of recombinant colonies by antibiotic resistance screening.
keyPoints: ori: initiates self-replication of plasmid in host; controls copy number
Restriction site: allows specific cutting for insertion of foreign DNA; within antibiotic genes for insertional inactivation

subject: Biology
text: Differentiate between exonuclease and endonuclease. In what context are restriction endonucleases used in biotechnology?
modelAnswer: Exonuclease: Cuts nucleotides from the ends (5' or 3') of a DNA strand sequentially. Endonuclease: Makes cuts within the DNA strand at specific internal sites. Restriction endonucleases are a type of endonuclease that recognise specific palindromic sequences and cut DNA at or near these sites, producing defined fragments. In biotechnology: used to cut vector DNA and foreign DNA at specific sites → both have compatible ends → ligated together to form recombinant DNA.
keyPoints: Restriction endonucleases: specific palindromic site recognition, produce defined fragments
Used to cut vector and insert for recombinant DNA formation

subject: Biology
text: Describe all stages of human insulin production through recombinant DNA technology. How does recombinant insulin differ from proinsulin?
modelAnswer: Stages: (1) Insulin gene (A chain and B chain) synthesised chemically; (2) Each gene inserted separately into plasmid vector (pBR322); (3) Recombinant plasmid introduced into E. coli; (4) E. coli expresses the gene, producing insulin chains; (5) A and B chains extracted, purified; (6) Chains joined by disulphide bonds in vitro → active human insulin (Humulin). Proinsulin vs insulin: Proinsulin (precursor) is a single polypeptide with A chain + C peptide + B chain. The C peptide is excised post-translationally, producing mature active insulin (A+B chains connected by two disulphide bonds).
keyPoints: A and B chains synthesised separately in E. coli
Chains purified and joined by disulphide bonds → Humulin
Proinsulin has extra C peptide removed post-translationally
No C peptide in mature insulin

subject: Biology
text: Give the full form of GEAC and state two important functions it performs.
modelAnswer: GEAC: Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (under the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change, Government of India). Two functions: (1) Makes decisions regarding the validity of GM research and safety of introducing GMOs for public use; (2) Approves large-scale use of GM crops and GM organisms after evaluating safety and biosafety data; (3) Regulates the use of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) in India.
keyPoints: Approves GM research and large-scale use of GMOs
Regulates biosafety of genetically modified organisms in India

subject: Biology
text: What is bio-piracy? Give the example of the turmeric patent case. What did the Indian Government do in response?
modelAnswer: Bio-piracy: The practice of multinationals/foreign companies patenting traditional knowledge or biological resources of other nations (usually developing countries) without proper authorization or compensation. Turmeric case: A US patent was granted for wound-healing property of turmeric (Curcuma longa) – a knowledge that Indians have used for centuries. Indian Government's response: The Indian government challenged the patent in the US Patent Office with evidence from ancient Sanskrit texts and old publications (prior art), and the patent was successfully revoked. India also drafted the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) to document traditional knowledge and prevent future bio-piracy.
keyPoints: Bio-piracy: patenting traditional knowledge without compensation
Turmeric: US patent for wound healing revoked by India using prior art evidence
TKDL created to document traditional knowledge

subject: Biology
text: What was Rosie, the transgenic cow? Why was her milk said to be nutritionally balanced?
modelAnswer: Rosie was the first transgenic cow (1997) produced with the human gene for alpha-lactalbumin inserted. Her milk contained human alpha-lactalbumin protein, making it nutritionally richer and more suitable for human babies than normal cow's milk. Her milk was said to be nutritionally balanced because human alpha-lactalbumin improves the whey protein composition of cow's milk, making it compositionally closer to human breast milk, providing better nutrition for infants.
keyPoints: Milk nutritionally richer/closer to human breast milk for infants

subject: Biology
text: Explain how transgenic animals can be beneficial to humans. Describe any three ways.
modelAnswer: (1) Normal physiology and development: Transgenic animals can be used to study how genes are regulated and how they affect normal body functions – e.g., how insulin gene is expressed and regulated. (2) Disease study: They are created as disease models (e.g., Alzheimer's mouse model) to study diseases for which no human studies are possible; helps in developing new drugs. (3) Biological products/pharmaceuticals: Human genes expressed in transgenic animals produce valuable proteins – e.g., Rosie (transgenic cow) produced human alpha-lactalbumin in milk; transgenic sheep Dolly's potential for producing drugs in milk. (4) Vaccine safety testing: Transgenic mice used to test safety of vaccines.
keyPoints: Study of gene regulation and normal physiology
Disease models for drug development (e.g., Alzheimer's mouse)

subject: Biology
text: Identify the type of interaction in: (i) Egret and cattle, (ii) Cuckoo and crow. Justify your answer.
modelAnswer: (i) Egret and cattle: Commensalism. The egret feeds on insects disturbed by the moving cattle (egret benefits), while cattle are neither harmed nor benefited. (ii) Cuckoo and crow: Brood parasitism. The cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) lays its eggs in the crow's nest; the crow (host) incubates the eggs and raises the cuckoo chick, which is detrimental to the crow's own offspring. The cuckoo benefits; the crow is harmed → parasitism.
keyPoints: Cuckoo lays eggs in crow nest; crow raises cuckoo chick

subject: Biology
text: Define carrying capacity of a species. Explain the logistic growth (S-shaped curve) with reference to carrying capacity.
modelAnswer: Carrying capacity (K): The maximum population size that a given environment can support indefinitely, given available resources (food, space, water). Logistic growth (S-shaped/sigmoidal curve): When resources are limited, population initially grows rapidly (J-shaped phase, like exponential), then growth rate slows as population approaches K (due to increased competition, predation, disease), and finally stabilizes at K. The equation is dN/dt = rN[(K–N)/K]. The curve has a lag phase, log phase, and a stationary phase at K.
keyPoints: K = maximum population sustainable by environment
Logistic growth: rapid early growth, slows near K, stabilizes at K

subject: Biology
text: Explain Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle with a suitable example.
modelAnswer: Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle: Two species competing for identical resources (same ecological niche) cannot coexist indefinitely. The competitively superior species will eventually exclude the other. Example: Paramecium aurelia and P. caudatum – when grown separately (in controlled lab conditions), both grew to their carrying capacity. When grown together competing for the same food resources, P. aurelia outcompeted P. caudatum, which declined and was eventually excluded. Only P. aurelia survived. This demonstrates that complete competitors cannot coexist.
keyPoints: Two species competing for same niche cannot coexist
Example: P. aurelia outcompetes P. caudatum
Resource partitioning allows similar species to coexist

subject: Biology
text: Define predation. Why is predation necessary (give two points)? Why are predators said to be 'prudent'?
modelAnswer: Predation: An interaction where one organism (predator) kills and eats another (prey) for energy. Why necessary: (1) Energy transfer across trophic levels – herbivores and carnivores transfer energy from plants upward in the food chain; (2) Population regulation – predators keep prey populations in check, preventing overexploitation of resources. Why predators are 'prudent': Predators typically do not exterminate their prey populations, because if prey becomes extinct, predators would also die. Natural selection favours predators that take only enough prey to survive – maintaining prey population for continued food supply. This self-regulating behaviour makes them 'prudent'.
keyPoints: Predation: predator kills prey for energy
Energy transfer between trophic levels; population regulation
Prudent: predators avoid driving prey extinct; self-regulation for food security

subject: Biology
text: Explain the level of biodiversity at genetic, species and ecological levels with one example each.
modelAnswer: Genetic diversity: Variation in genes within a species; individuals of the same species differ in their genetic makeup. Example: Rauwolfia vomitoria plants growing across the Himalayas show genetic variation in potency/concentration of reserpine. Species diversity: Variety of different species in an area. Example: Western Ghats have more amphibian species diversity than Eastern Ghats. Ecological diversity: Variety of ecosystems/biomes in a region. Example: India has rainforests, mangroves, deserts, grasslands, wetlands, coral reefs – high ecological diversity compared to a Scandinavian country.
keyPoints: Species: variety of species in an area (amphibians in Western Ghats)
Ecological: variety of ecosystems (India: rainforest, desert, mangroves)

subject: Biology
text: A population growth equation is: dN/dt = rN. (a) What type of growth model does this represent? (b) What does 'r' signify? (c) What curve is obtained if N is plotted against time? (d) Is resource availability limited or unlimited?
modelAnswer: (a) Exponential (J-shaped) growth model – also called Malthusian growth. (b) 'r' = intrinsic rate of natural increase (biotic potential) – the difference between birth rate (b) and death rate (d); r = b – d; represents the maximum growth rate under ideal conditions. (c) J-shaped (exponential) growth curve is obtained when N is plotted against time. (d) Resources are unlimited – exponential growth assumes food, space and other resources are not limiting, so population grows at a constant maximum rate.
keyPoints: r = intrinsic rate of natural increase (b - d)

subject: Biology
text: Explain the mutually rewarding relationship between the Yucca plant and the Yucca moth.
modelAnswer: The Yucca plant and the moth Tegeticula (Pronuba) species have an obligate mutualistic relationship: The moth pollinates Yucca flowers while laying its eggs inside the flower. The moth larvae feed on developing Yucca seeds. The Yucca can only be pollinated by this moth (no other pollinator works). Both species benefit – the plant is pollinated (reproduction assured) and the moth gets food for its larvae. Neither can survive without the other, making this an example of co-evolution.
keyPoints: Obligate mutualism between Yucca and Yucca moth
Moth pollinates Yucca flowers; lays eggs in flower

subject: Biology
text: Identify the type of ecological pyramid that is inverted. Give an example. State two limitations of ecological pyramids.
modelAnswer: Inverted pyramid: Pyramid of biomass in aquatic ecosystems (e.g., pond/sea) – biomass of producers (phytoplankton) is less than that of consumers (zooplankton, fish). Example: Phytoplankton (small biomass at any instant) → zooplankton (larger biomass). Two limitations: (1) Pyramids do not account for seasons, decomposers, or saprophytes; (2) They assume simple food chains and cannot represent food webs; (3) Pyramid of numbers ignores size of organisms (e.g., one large tree supports thousands of insects).
keyPoints: Pyramid of biomass is inverted in aquatic ecosystems
Limitations: ignore seasons/decomposers; cannot represent food webs

subject: Biology
text: What is primary productivity? How is it expressed? Explain the relationship: NPP = GPP – R.
modelAnswer: Primary productivity: The rate of organic matter (biomass) produced by producers (autotrophs/plants) per unit area per unit time through photosynthesis. Expressed as: g/m²/yr or kcal/m²/yr (weight or energy per unit area per year). GPP (Gross Primary Productivity): Total organic matter produced by plants. R: Energy used in plant respiration. NPP (Net Primary Productivity) = GPP – R: NPP is the organic matter remaining after the plant uses some for its own respiration; this NPP is available to herbivores and other consumers.
keyPoints: Primary productivity: rate of biomass production by autotrophs
NPP = GPP - R (respiration); available to next trophic level

subject: Biology
text: Differentiate between the grazing food chain and detritus food chain.
modelAnswer: Grazing Food Chain (GFC): Starts from living green plants (autotrophs). Energy flow: Plants → Herbivores → Carnivores. Example: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle. Energy source: Solar energy fixed by photosynthesis. Detritus Food Chain (DFC): Starts from dead organic matter (detritus/litter). Energy flow: Dead organic matter → Detritivores (fungi, bacteria) → Detritivore predators. Example: Leaf litter → Earthworm → Robin. Energy source: Chemical energy stored in dead organic matter. In terrestrial ecosystems DFC dominates; in aquatic systems GFC dominates.
keyPoints: GFC: starts from living plants; solar energy
DFC: starts from dead organic matter; chemical energy

subject: Biology
text: Explain stratification in a forest ecosystem. Why do different species occupy different levels?
modelAnswer: Stratification: The vertical distribution of different species at different levels (layers) in an ecosystem. In a forest: (1) Top canopy (emergent) layer – tall trees receiving maximum sunlight; (2) Canopy layer – medium trees; (3) Understory/sub-canopy – smaller trees in shade; (4) Shrub layer – shade-tolerant shrubs; (5) Herb/ground layer – grasses, mosses in deep shade; (6) Forest floor – decomposers, detritivores. Reason: Different species are adapted to different light intensities, temperatures and humidity levels at each stratum; resource partitioning (each species exploits a different niche), reducing competition and increasing species diversity.
keyPoints: Vertical layers: emergent canopy, canopy, understory, shrub, herb, ground
Different species adapted to different light/temperature

subject: Biology
text: Compare decomposition rates in two soil samples – one with dried leaves (lignin-rich) and one with fresh fruit peels. What is the effect of lignin and cutin on decomposition rate?
modelAnswer: Fresh fruit peels (low lignin, high soluble sugars): Decompose rapidly – decomposers (bacteria and fungi) easily break down simple organic compounds; high moisture content accelerates decomposition. Dried lignin-rich leaves: Decompose slowly – lignin is a complex aromatic polymer very resistant to enzymatic breakdown; fewer microbes can digest it. Effect of lignin and cutin: These complex structural polymers (lignin in wood/leaves; cutin in plant cuticle) are resistant to decomposition because their complex chemical bonds are difficult for most decomposers to break. They reduce decomposition rate and contribute to humus formation.
keyPoints: Fresh fruit peels: high moisture, simple organics → rapid decomposition
Lignin-rich leaves: complex polymer resistant to breakdown → slow decomposition
Lignin and cutin are recalcitrant → reduce decomposition rate → form humus

subject: Biology
text: State the effects of loss of biodiversity (two points) and two major causes of biodiversity loss.
modelAnswer: Effects of biodiversity loss: (1) Decline in ecosystem services – reduced productivity, pollination, water purification, flood control; (2) Loss of potential resources – pharmaceutical compounds, food sources, industrial materials from yet-unexplored species; (3) Reduced ecosystem stability and resilience. Two major causes of biodiversity loss: (1) Habitat destruction and fragmentation – deforestation, urbanisation, agriculture expansion; (2) Overexploitation – hunting, poaching, overfishing; (3) Invasive species introduction; (4) Climate change.
keyPoints: Loss of ecosystem services; loss of potential resources

subject: Biology
text: What are sacred groves? In which category of conservation do they fall? How do they help in biodiversity conservation?
modelAnswer: Sacred groves: Patches of forest set aside and protected by local communities due to religious and cultural traditions; considered sacred to a deity or ancestral spirit. Category: In-situ conservation. Help in conservation: (1) Strict protection from cutting, hunting and disturbance means these forest patches become refuges for rare and endangered species; (2) They preserve traditional knowledge of local plants; (3) In Meghalaya (Jaintia and Khasi hills) sacred groves (Law Lyngdoh) protect many rare orchids and ferns; (4) They protect watersheds and prevent soil erosion.
keyPoints: Patches of forest protected by local communities for religious/cultural reasons
Protect rare/endangered species; preserve biodiversity hotspots

subject: Biology
text: Name four advanced methods of ex-situ conservation. Where are animals that have become extinct in the wild maintained?
modelAnswer: Four advanced ex-situ conservation methods: (1) Cryopreservation – preservation of gametes/embryos/seeds at very low temperatures (–196°C in liquid nitrogen) in gene banks; (2) In vitro fertilisation followed by embryo transfer; (3) Tissue culture / propagation of plants; (4) Captive breeding in zoological parks (zoos). Animals extinct in the wild are maintained in: Zoological parks (zoos). Other places: Wildlife sanctuaries, botanical gardens (for plants), seed banks, cryopreservation facilities.
keyPoints: Animals extinct in wild kept in zoological parks

subject: Biology
text: State two characteristics of a biodiversity hotspot. Why is India considered a megadiverse country?
modelAnswer: Two characteristics of a biodiversity hotspot: (1) Contains at least 1,500 species of endemic vascular plants (high endemism); (2) Has lost more than 70% of its original habitat (under serious threat). India as megadiverse: India has over 8.1% of global species diversity despite covering only 2.4% of the world's land area; has 2 biodiversity hotspots (Western Ghats and Indo-Burma hotspot); is among the 17 mega-diverse countries; has high diversity at species, genetic and ecosystem levels.
keyPoints: Hotspot: ≥1500 endemic vascular plant species; >70% habitat lost
India: 8.1% global species in 2.4% land area

subject: Biology
text: Region A has sustained high fever, stomach pain, constipation and loss of appetite. Region B shows inflammation in lower limbs and genital organs. Identify the diseases in each region.
modelAnswer: Region A: Typhoid (Typhoid fever / Enteric fever) caused by Salmonella typhi. Symptoms: sustained high fever (39–40°C), abdominal pain, constipation, loss of appetite; sometimes rose spots on skin. Region B: Filariasis (Elephantiasis) caused by the filarial worm Wuchereria bancrofti. The filarial worms block lymphatic vessels, causing accumulation of lymph → massive inflammation and enlargement of lower limbs, feet and genital organs.
keyPoints: Region A: Typhoid (Salmonella typhi) – fever, abdominal pain, constipation
Region B: Filariasis/elephantiasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) – lymphatic blockage, swollen limbs

subject: Biology
text: A person smokes cigarettes. Describe: (i) the effect of nicotine on blood pressure and heart rate, (ii) the effect of CO on haemoglobin, (iii) the pharmacological class of nicotine and one other drug in the same class.
modelAnswer: (i) Nicotine stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline, which increase heart rate, blood pressure and raise blood glucose. This increases cardiovascular workload and risk of coronary artery disease. (ii) Carbon monoxide (CO) from cigarette smoke has 200× greater affinity for haemoglobin than oxygen. CO binds to Hb forming carboxyhaemoglobin (CoHb), which cannot carry oxygen. This reduces blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, causing oxygen deprivation of tissues. (iii) Nicotine is a stimulant (acts on CNS/nervous system; stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors). Another drug in same class: cocaine (also a CNS stimulant).
keyPoints: Nicotine → adrenaline release → increased BP and heart rate
CO binds Hb 200x stronger than O2 → carboxyhaemoglobin → reduced O2 transport
Nicotine = stimulant; cocaine is another stimulant

subject: Biology
text: Explain the study of plant evolution from the chart: (a) Which plant is the immediate ancestor of both ferns and conifers? (b) Name nearest ancestors of flowering plants. (c) Name the most primitive plant group. (d) Which classes does Psilophyton provide common ancestry to? (e) Common ancestor of Psilophyton and seed ferns? (f) Common ancestor of mosses and tracheophytes?
modelAnswer: (a) Psilophyton – acts as immediate ancestor of both ferns and conifers. (b) Seed ferns (Pteridosperms) are the nearest ancestors of flowering plants (Angiosperms). (c) Chlorophyte ancestors (green algae) – the most primitive (ancient) group. (d) Psilophyton provides common ancestry to ferns and conifers (and seed ferns). (e) Tracheophyte ancestors – common ancestor of Psilophyton and seed ferns. (f) Chlorophyte ancestors – common ancestor of mosses and tracheophytes.
keyPoints: Psilophyton = ancestor of ferns and conifers
Seed ferns = nearest ancestor of flowering plants
Tracheophyte ancestors = ancestor of Psilophyton and seed ferns; Chlorophyte = ancestor of mosses and tracheophytes

subject: Biology
text: Explain how Agrobacterium is used to protect tobacco plants from attack by nematode (Meloidogyne incognita).
modelAnswer: Meloidogyne incognita is a nematode that infects tobacco plant roots. RNA interference (RNAi) strategy using Agrobacterium: (1) Genes from the nematode (specific to nematode survival) are identified; (2) These genes are cloned in both sense and antisense orientation in a Ti plasmid-based vector in Agrobacterium; (3) Agrobacterium is used to introduce this construct into tobacco plant cells; (4) Inside the infected plant, the nematode-specific gene is transcribed from both orientations producing dsRNA; (5) This dsRNA triggers RNAi – silencing of the nematode's gene in its cells via mRNA degradation → nematode cannot survive in the transgenic tobacco roots.
keyPoints: Nematode-specific gene cloned in sense and antisense in Ti plasmid vector
dsRNA produced → RNAi silences nematode gene → nematode dies

subject: Biology
text: Expand ELISA. On which principle is the ELISA test based? Explain the process.
modelAnswer: ELISA: Enzyme Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay. Principle: It is based on antigen-antibody interaction. A specific antibody linked to an enzyme binds to the target antigen; the enzyme catalyses a colour-producing reaction, making detection possible. Process: (1) Antigen (e.g., pathogen protein) is coated on a microplate well; (2) Patient's serum (sample) is added; if specific antibodies are present, they bind to the antigen; (3) A secondary antibody linked to an enzyme (e.g., HRP) is added → binds to primary antibody; (4) Substrate for the enzyme is added → colour change. Colour intensity (measured by spectrophotometer) indicates the amount of antigen/antibody – positive result confirms infection.
keyPoints: Enzyme-linked antibody produces colour on substrate
Used to detect HIV, hepatitis, hormones, allergens

subject: Biology
text: Describe the interaction between fig tree and wasps: (a) Name the type of interaction. (b) What benefits do female wasps get? (c) Give one other example of animal-plant co-evolution.
modelAnswer: (a) Mutualism – both the fig tree and the wasp benefit. (b) Female wasps: lay eggs inside the fig flower (inverted inflorescence); the fig provides a protected site for egg-laying and the larvae feed on some fig seeds → wasp reproduction is assured. (c) Other example of co-evolution: Yucca plant and Yucca moth – the moth pollinates Yucca flowers while laying eggs in the flower; larvae eat some Yucca seeds. Both partners benefit and have co-evolved (neither can reproduce without the other).
keyPoints: Wasp benefits: protected egg-laying site, larvae fed by fig seeds

subject: Biology
text: Describe the translation process in protein synthesis.
modelAnswer: Translation: The process of synthesis of a polypeptide chain from an mRNA sequence at ribosomes. Stages: (1) Initiation: Ribosome (small subunit) binds to mRNA at the start codon (AUG); initiator tRNA (Met-tRNA) binds the P-site; large subunit joins. (2) Elongation: Aminoacyl-tRNA binds A-site (anticodon matches mRNA codon); peptide bond formed by peptidyl transferase (rRNA); ribosome translocates by one codon (tRNA moves P→E→exit). (3) Termination: Stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) reaches A-site; release factor binds; polypeptide released; ribosome dissociates from mRNA.
keyPoints: Initiation: small subunit binds mRNA at AUG; initiator Met-tRNA; large subunit joins
Elongation: aminoacyl-tRNA binds A-site; peptide bond; translocation
Termination: stop codon; release factor; polypeptide released

subject: Biology
text: Answer the following: (a) Specific location of vasa efferentia and vas deferens in male reproductive system. (b) What is a polar body? When is the first polar body produced? (c) What is the fate of the Graafian follicle after ovulation?
modelAnswer: (a) Vasa efferentia: a network of tubules carrying sperm from rete testis to the epididymis (within the testis-epididymis junction). Vas deferens: extends from the epididymis (tail), loops over the urinary bladder, and joins the duct of seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct. (b) Polar body: A small non-functional cell produced during meiosis in oogenesis. It receives very little cytoplasm. First polar body produced: during Meiosis I, when the primary oocyte divides → secondary oocyte + 1st polar body (within Graafian follicle, just before ovulation). (c) After ovulation, the ruptured Graafian follicle transforms into corpus luteum (under LH influence), which secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrium during early pregnancy. If no fertilization, corpus luteum degenerates → corpus albicans.
keyPoints: Vasa efferentia: rete testis to epididymis; vas deferens: epididymis to ejaculatory duct
Polar body: small non-functional cell from meiosis; 1st produced during meiosis I
Graafian follicle → corpus luteum (secretes progesterone) → corpus albicans

subject: Biology
text: Answer: (a) Where do coleoptile and coleorhiza appear in a monocot seed? (b) What is free nuclear endosperm? Give an example. (c) What are parthenocarpic fruits? Give an example.
modelAnswer: (a) Coleoptile: a sheath covering and protecting the plumule (shoot apex) of monocot embryo; it pierces the soil during germination. Coleorhiza: a sheath covering the radicle of monocot embryo; present around the root cap and root. (b) Free nuclear endosperm: In early development, nuclear divisions occur without cell wall formation, producing a large number of free nuclei; cell wall formation occurs later. Example: Coconut water (liquid endosperm) represents free nuclear stage. (c) Parthenocarpic fruits: Fruits developed from the ovary without fertilization; they are seedless. Example: Banana (naturally parthenocarpic); seedless grapes, seedless watermelon.
keyPoints: Coleoptile covers plumule; coleorhiza covers radicle in monocots
Free nuclear endosperm: nuclear divisions without cell wall initially; example: coconut water
Parthenocarpy: fruit without fertilization, seedless; example: banana
